context_documents.title: 2022-4911 · A six-bar collector and configurable CAD need version-aware interpretation
context_documents.body:
# 2022-4911: A six-bar collector and configurable CAD need version-aware interpretation

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The reveal describes a six-bar pickup with knockdown rollers for bouncing cargo, adjustable launcher rails/top roller and traversal climb. The later CAD release explicitly includes a configuration for the original Glacier Peak climb.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The stated roller purpose is controlling bouncing balls and the rail/top-contact purpose includes a broad shooting envelope with reduced unwanted spin. Exact design-choice causation beyond that is not established.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A configurable assembly can preserve genuine history, but the default displayed CAD is not automatically the configuration used at every event. Knockdown and acquisition contacts should be tested together; a roller that stops bounce may also create a pinch.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Inspect both CAD configurations and validate bouncing-entry behavior plus disabled climb retention.

## Limits

First-party release topics 404720 and 412974; no technical-video rewatch claimed. Reveal text and topic title use differing names, so source naming is preserved rather than silently harmonized.

source_reviews.title: CyberKnights SLAPSHOT and QUICKDROP reveal
source_reviews.review_basis: Read the authored Discourse post bodies and attachment metadata.
facts: Original six-bar, launcher and Mk4i disclosure.
Reports Glacier Peak failures, NU replacement and timed 3.2-second scoring position versus 4.2-second full release.
source_reviews.limitations: The time is a team demonstration. Image attachments and linked videos were not visually inspected.

source_reviews.title: CyberKnights QUICKDROP CAD release
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team-authored post bodies and attachment URLs.
facts: CAD has an original-climber configuration. Distance-shot tuning followed Sammamish.
source_reviews.limitations: CAD geometry and attachment pixels were not inspected.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: CyberKnights started the season as SLAPSHOT and renamed the redesigned robot QUICKDROP before Sammamish. The change was principally a new climb and lower center of mass, after repeated failures at Glacier Peak exposed differences between the home fixture and the competition bars. A separate intake impact prompted removal of the knockdown rollers. Meanwhile the adjustable launcher had already worked mechanically and the team later expanded its calibrated use.
piece_flow: The original six-bar used auxiliary knockdown rollers to control bouncing cargo. The team removed those rollers during Glacier Peak after collision damage.
The release text establishes the adjustable-rail launcher with a powered top roller, but the intermediate storage and feed contacts remain unresolved.
The fender shot was the early calibrated solution. Longer shots became available after tuning between Sammamish and district championship.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: SDS Mk4i swerve provided the base. The new climber lowered the center of mass according to the team, reducing one consequence of concentrating the climb hardware high. Any reproduction needs both the parked envelope and the changing suspended envelope. The published assembly has a setting for the original climber, so a screenshot alone needs a configuration label.

subsystems.name: Six-bar collector
subsystems.construction: Six-bar with knockdown contacts in the original reveal. The failure report refers to belts and a polycarbonate roller tube.
subsystems.operation: Acquire moving or bouncing cargo. The auxiliary rollers were removed after an impact and the team continued with the rest of the intake.
subsystems.team_rationale: The extra contacts were intended for bounce control. They were lower priority than making the climb reliable after Week 1.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A useful auxiliary contact should have an impact load path that does not pull the primary drive belt off or shear a shared attachment.
subsystems.interfaces: Map stowed and deployed roller geometry against bumper coverage and the belt route.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: The team reported thrown belts and sheared fasteners. Compare operation with and without the auxiliary contact after a controlled offset hit.
subsystems.unknowns: Final reinstallation status and detailed feeder geometry are unresolved.

subsystems.name: Adjustable rail launcher
subsystems.construction: Adjustable rails and a powered top roller intended to limit spin.
subsystems.operation: Use the fender preset first and add distance shooting once the mechanism and camera calibration are ready.
subsystems.team_rationale: Late access to the robot forced the software team to prioritize basic operation, autonomous and driver practice. The team says the hood needed no design changes or substantial maintenance.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Shot range capability is the intersection of mechanical range and calibrated aim. A reliable adjustment mechanism can be worth preserving while postponing broad calibration.
subsystems.interfaces: A moving hood must preserve consistent cargo entry over its range. Vision quality and operator practice affect whether the extra range is useful.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Repeat the fender test with deliberate misalignment and check longer shots separately after vision interruption.
subsystems.unknowns: No verified shot table, throughput measurement or transport sequence.

subsystems.name: SLAPSHOT and QUICKDROP climbs
subsystems.construction: The original traversal system preceded a team-designed 125-inspired NU skip-high-bar climber. The later mid-bar arms could backdrive in the published demonstration.
subsystems.operation: Establish support at mid, reach traversal without a high-bar transfer and allow mid-arm release after traversal capture.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team reported five early falls and much greater field-bar flex than at home. It credited the new geometry with lowering the center of mass and reducing climb time.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Bar compliance changes chassis motion and hook position together. Test flexible and stiff fixtures, and distinguish time to secure scoring position from time to full release.
subsystems.interfaces: The bar, hook attitude, chassis mass and disabled behavior govern the full transition.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check one-sided capture, release with motors disabled, and loads on stops and camera mounts after a fall.
subsystems.unknowns: The demonstration times are not a measured field success distribution.

revisions: Removed knockdown rollers at Glacier Peak. Replaced climber before Sammamish and renamed the robot. Reported a later full teardown and minor changes before district championship.
transferable_principles: Use a field-like support fixture for dynamic mechanism testing.
Track hardware readiness separately from controls and practice readiness.
disconfirming_conditions: Skip-bar geometry can lose its speed benefit if compliance and alignment shrink its capture window.
A passively backdrivable release is only useful if the scoring state and retained support remain valid with power removed.
remaining_gaps: Exact restored intake state, intervening storage geometry, CAD measurements and independent climb reliability.

recommended_images.caption: Exact original attached image from the team’s QUICKDROP CAD release. Inspect to confirm view and configuration before embedding.
Exact Google Photos video preview linked in the QUICKDROP redesign announcement. Verify robot and usable framing before embedding.
